extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on point of view, tense, and descriptive technique for fiction — how to choose and sustain POV, use tense and time distance, and create vivid, specific sensory description with precise word choice, figurative language, and sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense choice and time distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tense deliberately: present tense can make narration feel more immediate, while past tense is a long-standing convention that readers often find 'invisible'; specifying events as having occurred long ago creates time distance that may reduce suspense but can add nostalgia or a reflective perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present-tense example: Margaret Atwood's Surfacing to increase immediacy. Time-distance example: George Eliot's 'The Lifted Veil'—opening in a far future/premortem voice reduces suspense but allows retrospective perspective. Consider how tense and stated chronology shape urgency, reliability, and emotional tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: POV contract / consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view establishes a contract with the reader: it tells the reader what kind of story they are reading; breaking the contract risks losing the reader's trust and the story's realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not slip into another character's consciousness if you've chosen a single-vision limited POV. Example anti-pattern: a third-person-limited story suddenly entering a minor character's thoughts (student example). Fix by reporting other characters' actions and dialogue rather than their internal thoughts. Deliberate POV breaks are possible but should be intentional and serve a clear effect (examples: Richard Russo's controlled shifts). As a safeguard, write down your POV rules regarding omniscience, reliability, and distance, and check each paragraph against them when revising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting appropriate point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the POV that belongs to 'whose story' it is: single dominant character often calls for first-person or third-person limited; stories about groups or ensembles may need multiple-vision or a spokesperson POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'Whose story is this?' and 'What am I most interested in showing?' Taste a POV by writing a page or two to see how it feels on the page. Be willing to change POV in revision if another voice better serves the story (author anecdote: rewrote first-person novel into third-person single-vision and improved tone & flexibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain continuity and vividness (the 'continuous dream')
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a vivid and continuous 'dream' for the reader so the fictional world feels as sharp and immersive as real life; do not allow the reader's mind to wander out of the fictional world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think filmically: description is what envelops readers. Keep images and sensory detail consistent so the story reads like a continuous movie rather than a flickering or fading projection. Avoid jolts that break immersion (e.g., inconsistent voice, POV slips, or abrupt tense changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory detail (all five senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring readers into the fictional world, offer data for all five senses — sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch — not only visual detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on non-visual senses can be especially powerful (exercise: write a pitch-dark spelunking scene using hearing, smell, touch, taste). Examples: Faulkner and Amy Tan passages that combine smell, sight, sound, and tactile sensations. Sensory details should support and ground any abstract or poetic statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and concrete detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions must be specific rather than vague; specific sensory details accumulate to create verisimilitude and make settings and characters believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague descriptors like 'intense gray eyes' or 'she was a beautiful blonde' without concrete qualifiers. Name exact colors, fabrics, objects, places, and small particulars (examples: Jeannette Winterson's green hair with slime; Louis B. Jones's street directions and paint color). Use lists of names/catalogs when appropriate (Barbara Kingsolver example). Learn names for trees, materials, colors to notch up clarity. Brand names can be useful but overuse can distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice and vocabulary precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the best possible word to convey your image or sensation; the difference between the right word and the almost-right word can be enormous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a dictionary and thesaurus handy; broaden your vocabulary so you can choose precise nouns and verbs (Mark Twain quote cited). Select words that sustain the magical illusion of the story; consider why an author chooses a particular word (example: 'a string of cats' versus 'collection'—the connotation matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize strong nouns and verbs; minimize reliance on modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong nouns and verbs carry more descriptive power than adjectives and adverbs; when nouns and verbs are vivid, modifiers are often unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fitzgerald's 'seizes' and 'dumps' vs weaker phrasing; Melanie Rae Thon and Arundhati Roy examples showing forceful nouns and dynamic verbs. Transform adverb-reliant phrases into stronger verbs (e.g., 'she walked lightly' -> 'she glided'). Focus first on finding the best nouns/verbs, then add modifiers only as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adjectives and adverbs sparingly and purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives and adverbs are helper words (modifiers) that can be useful in small doses but often indicate lazy description when overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid piling on modifiers ('She walked gracefully into the spacious room, swiftly removing a letter from her designer-label purse and regarding us all with her intense gray eyes.') — this yields little concrete image. Well-placed modifiers can work (example: 'silent' in Winterson sentence). The 'no-adjective/adverb' exercise (describe someone without adjectives/adverbs) can strengthen noun/verb choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figurative language (similes and metaphors) fresh and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes and metaphors are powerful shorthand for conveying imagery and emotional resonances; prefer fresh, surprising figures of speech over clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similes are flexible and can be used in many contexts (dialogue, first-person, headlines); metaphors can be weightier and can carry an extended allegorical frame (Kafka example). Examples of effective fresh figurative language: Mary Gaitskill, Calvin Baker. Avoid hackneyed expressions used unthinkingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyricism, rhythm, and sound in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose that attends to rhythm, sound, and musicality (lyricism) deepens reader immersion and can convey meanings beyond literal diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read your work aloud to hear ebb and flow and locate clunks. Lyricism does not require long sentences — Hemingway's short, chantlike rhythms show this. Examples: James Joyce's 'The Dead' line for lyricism; Hemingway's imagery for simple lyricism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onomatopoeia and sonic detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words that mimic sounds (onomatopoeia) and explicit sonic detail to make scenes more immediate and physical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include murmurs, buzzes, hisses, clunks where appropriate to convey auditory texture. The text notes 'clunk' as an example and suggests leveraging sound words to deepen sensory experience.
